There’s just a few things left. I’ll get the deposit back. They’ll hand me the check, and I’ll hand it to him. Then it’ll be over.
My stomach's cramping.
James would definitely bring food if I asked—probably show up with an entire Erewhon sushi platter, acting like I still deserved the royal treatment.
And real sushi sounds so good. Almost worth all the bullshit that would come with it. The last thing I ordered was one of those cheap California rolls, the kind with fake crab meat dyed neon orange.

The delivery guy told me that the neon orange dye they use is made from crushed-up bugs. They mash them into a paste, soak your food in it, and call it luxury. Probably said it because I didn’t leave him a tip.
And yet, here I am, reduced to craving fish paste drenched in bug juice.
It’s all just chemicals anyway, probably no worse than half the shit I’ve smoked.

I just need to trash the rest of this life. Tear it apart, burn it down, whatever it takes to start fresh. The faster I work, the closer I get to that $3,000 and the closer I am to eating something that doesn’t taste like a fucking lie.
I don’t even know what I’m grabbing anymore. Toothpaste, hand towels, dishes with stupid little ducks on them that my mom said I couldn't throw away. I just need them gone.
Everything goes over. Everything gets sucked up by the void.
And then. I’m holding the last of it.

Everyone has an irreplaceable box, and this one is mine. Useless shit that, somehow, has collectively become the most defining set of physical objects I own. The ring that James wouldn't take back, the letters my mother wrote to me when I was a lonely freshman, childhood photos that I told myself were lame, and at the bottom, my first and only sobriety chip from AA.
Now I’m standing in the dark, perching on broken glass, bleeding from my big toe because my lamp is in a stupid tree and somehow there's glass everywhere.
And I can't stop feeling.
And no amount of adrenaline or freezing water is gonna stop it this time.
And I’m holding the box over the edge.
Why can't I ever see the stars?
Everything hurts.
My arm is shaking and I'm beginning to think that maybe I’m one of those poor things, one of those sad souls just like Devin.

Only I don’t have a mom to steal from or fight with. I don’t have someone to make it all better, because it’s broken. I’m broken. And I wish I hadn’t loved her so fucking much. So much that it still burns, even now.
365 days later, and I still can’t stand the weight of it.
I can see the blood stains all over the carpet. Hope that doesn’t count against my deposit. How much does it cost to clean up blood? It’s LA. It’s probably included in my lease.
My hand won’t stop twitching, and all I want to do is drop it. The box. My memories. All the things that make me feel worse about being so terrible.
Drop it. “Fucking drop it.” And even though I’m screaming, no one is listening to me.
Sobriety has made everything so much worse.
I don't feel clean. I feel dirty. My stomach bulges with bubble guts. I’m bleeding, cut up from the roof of my mouth to the bottom of my soul. Too sad for even my own self pity to save me.
Quitting drugs feels more like failure than failure ever did.
But I don't want to die young. I want to die old and rich and full of cool stories that don't include this one.
And it's suddenly impossible to ignore the smell of molding carpet, the broken glass, the bloody footprints.
And I know. I just know that there isn't going to be a check coming for me.
I wasn't there when she died. She was so mad at me that day. Furious. I was high. The good kind. The early kind, when drugs were still fun.
And I hate that I wasn't there to tell her. That I wasn’t there to make it better for her the way she made my whole life better for me.
I was just so damn scared I’d end up in that same bed someday.

I throw it—the box, the last bit of me I have left. But it doesn’t vanish into the black hole like I wanted. Instead, it shatters on the ground, and everything I am spills everywhere. I can see pictures of us, my mom and me, grinning, sunburned arms slung around each other on a beach somewhere. And I can’t stand it anymore. I can’t stand missing you this much. I want to go away again.
But I can’t stop looking. That memory—it’s still bright, still alive. I hold it close, clutching it to my filthy chest, right above the scar on my breast.
I’m crying. Really crying. Choking on snot and spit.
My little broken life is scattered on the ground. I grab at the pieces, covering myself with the papers and photos. I can’t find the ring. Where the fuck is James’s ring?
I search on my hands and knees for a few minutes before giving up.
More time goes by. I’ve made a blanket of all the things that I love most, but it isn’t enough.
And I pick up my goddam phone and it’s me that calls this time.
“James.”
“Jesus. Allie, Are you okay? I’ve been trying to reach you.”
“I know.”
“What's going on? Please just talk to me.”
And for the first time in a long time, I want to.
“Do you want to go get sushi?”

title: The Flying Nun
logline: A turbulent flight becomes a chaotic test of one deeply imperfect passenger’s capacity for heroism.

blocks.text: I had to pee and I was afraid to die, in that order. The plane was bucking hard over the Atlantic, scaring the hell out of everyone. The airline seat was hard, unforgiving, upholstered with something that even the most generous pricks would struggle to call leather. I stuck to the thing, sweating and clenching. Trying to hold it all in. Every lurch made my sphincter squeeze in panic. The grip was so intense, I could have cracked a turd in half. Despite all the goddamn fear, my bladder wouldn't let up.
"I can hold it," I assured myself.

But this shit show was budget—no in-flight movies, no tiny bottles of tequila to keep you sane. Nothing but the endless drone of engines and the jarring shake that rippled through the cabin, reminding all of us cheap bastards that we’d royally screwed ourselves.Carol would probably have called this Karma at 30,000 feet.I checked my pockets for the third time. I rubbed the little metal flask that had been empty since we boarded.
What I wouldn't give to keep from dying sober.
I mean dying is one thing, but sober and in a pool of my own piss? I had higher hopes.
My only saving grace?
Right next to me was the hottest nun you’ve ever seen. Her lips, God, her lips. Wet, wide, juicy little suckers I couldn’t stop staring at.
She was wearing the outfit and everything. They let her board early, right along with the screaming babies and that guy who insisted being over 65 counted as a disability. I admired her game.

My ex, Carol, hated nuns. Thought they were all brownnosers. But to be fair, her hate wasn’t exactly selective. She hated our house in Reno, my mother, her mother, her job, my job, the 15 years we spent together.
And me. She definitely hated me.

On the next jolt, the nun let out a soft little gasp, her tongue flicking out just enough to catch the fervent religious spittle gathering at the corner of her mouth. She’d been praying non-stop for the last ten minutes.
Every jostle, every shake, was met with the sweetest Hail Mary, full of grace. God probably didn’t have a clue what to do in a situation like this.
Tank the plane, and I go under. No great loss.
Then again, tank the plane, and his sweet little angel gets her first taste of water sports.
She glanced over at me, her knuckles bright white around around her thick little rosary.
“Would you like to pray with me?”
“Hell yeah.”
Her hand reached out, laying those soft, pink, moist little nubs gently over my fingers. I wanted to lick the holy sweat from her palms. Only, I don’t think my bladder could take another drop.
We caught a nasty gust of wind, and I tried to give her a reassuring wink—just as a nervous fart slipped out.
Surely she wouldn’t hold a bit of turbulence-induced flatulence against a fellow child of God.
“Close your eyes,” she whispered. “Let’s ask for his forgiveness.”
Close my eyes? Not a shot. Not when I could watch her mouth do the lord's work.
But then she froze. Her lips parted, those flushed red cheeks going green as her eyes widened in alarm. Her hand jerked away, clutching at her stomach.
She leaned forward, her eyes darting around in panic, desperately scanning for one of those emergency spew sacks.
I dug into the seat pockets in front of me, elbow deep in crumpled magazines, sticky wrappers, chewed up pen caps, loose pretzels, and a disturbing large clump of hair.
Guess barf bags are too good for economy.
“Hold on!” I screamed.
But God had other plans. She was about to blow, and on instinct, I reached out, my hand covering her mouth, her breath hot and damp against my skin.
Our eyes met and for a moment I got lost in those baby blues as the first wave of bile hit. It splattered against my skin, clinging to the creases of my palm.
I held firm, determined to be her savior as hot mucus threatened to slide through my fingers.
Slowly, she began to swallow, her throat moving in deliberate, rhythmic motions.

God may hate me. Just like he hated my father, my brother, my uncle, my second and third aunts, and that guy at the end of the cul-de-sac who kept getting arrested for DMT. But right then? I felt the call.

We had an Angel in common and she needed help. Needed tissues. Needed a nice, safe place to unburden herself. And if I could piss at the same time, well, that’s a two-for-one miracle if I ever saw one.
So I unbuckled, climbed over the holy spirit, and staggered toward the john. Determined to bring back the goods.
I’m talking barf bags, tissues, water bottles, headphones, blankets, ginger ale, those fancy inflatable pillows reserved for frequent flyers.

The stewardess, who was strapped in tight, shot me a thumbs down as I lurched across the cabin. She might've also been shouting at me to sit the hell down, but my bladder was screaming louder, so I didn't really give a shit.

Just then, a bout of turbulence flicked the lights off and a chorus of screams provided the perfect distraction. I ran, stumbling, to the back, shouldering the bathroom door with a hell of a lot of force.

My armpit caught the sticky edge of the Vacant sign and I felt some of the dangly squatters underneath my pit being ripped out as the pressure slid the door sideways. I fumbled in the dim light for the lock as the plane gave another violent shudder. The walls pulsated as I leaned against the cool metal, struggling to catch my breath.

Then the lights clicked on, and I wish to God they hadn't. The bathroom was a mess. I’m talking pure chaos. The turbulence had given everything a hellish shake-up. Pink soap was drizzled with artistic flair over the rim of the toilet seat. Several used tampons had liberated themselves from the sanitary bin, inching along the piss-soaked floor like a procession of eager, pre-metamorphosed caterpillars. Wads of toilet paper clung to the mirror, fused by clear clumps of creamy fluid that could have passed for snot but looked more like jizz.

The steel wing tipped, launching me sideways, and I stumbled, my foot skidding on the cluster of bloodied tampons. My hand shot out to brace my fall, landing in a slick smear of pink soap that sent me sliding forward, ramming the side of my face against the filthy toilet rimMy knees met solid ground, the urine soaking through my jeans.
Out of options, I interlaced my fingers in front of that toilet and appealed to a higher authority.
Dear God.

Please give me the strength to help that ridiculously hot nun in 3B. I know I’m not your favorite, I know I screwed things up with Carol. I wasn’t patient enough, I drank too much, and okay, I might’ve called her mother a bitch one too many times. But you’ve gotta admit, she really is a bitch.
The plane dropped suddenly. A quick, stomach-flipping plunge that sent my forehead bouncing off the rim of the toilet.
Look, if you can just grant me the decency to piss, I swear I’ll do everything I can to honor, cherish, and assist that divine piece of ass you’ve seated beside me. Amen.

Maybe it was divine intervention. Maybe it was just what a man has to do when faced with the defining moment of his life. When he has to choose between cowardice and courage, between pissing himself and becoming the master of his own destiny.
Determined, clutching the sink for support, I hauled my ass up.
Scuzzy hands went to adjust my fly, only to find it already hanging open. I hoped the nun hadn’t seen.

I didn’t have it in me to be embarrassed as I let go, relief washing over me with what might have been the most satisfying piss of my life. A good piss is a good piss, no matter the decor, but this was something else. Urine shot out of me with the force of a man half my age. Not too shabby, I thought, as my aim rang true, hitting the bowl’s sweet spot.

The sink was busted, so I wiped my hands, covered in shit, piss, grime, filth, and God knows what else, on wads of tissues I grabbed by the fistful. Some of them fell like breadcrumbs behind me as I stumbled toward the galley, where I was sure supplies for first-class passengers were stashed. My sticky hands jammed into cold metal compartments, hunting through pristine napkins, unopened wipes, lily-white vomit vessels—the kind of shit they don’t waste on the likes of economy flyers.
I grabbed it all by the handful.

The turbulence intensified as I stumbled past my fellow passengers, the plane bucking back and forth. I didn’t bother with the excuse mes or pardon mes, knocking into shoulders and knees, tripping over displaced limbs sprawled across the aisle.
I caught a glimpse of the promised land. My nun, just a dozen or so seats away.
A woman to my right barfed.II turned my head, and our eyes met. That same disgusted look, that streak of orange vomit tangled in her hair. God, I miss Carol.
Then the smell hit. A one two punch right to the old nasal passages. For a moment, I just stood there, stunned.
Seconds later it began.
A chain reaction—left, right, front, back—a chorus of puking on all sides.

It was at that moment I understood. God was giving me a second chance, a re-baptism of sorts. I couldn’t change all the times I’d let Carol down, all the chances I’d wasted to do right by my fellow man. But right now, in the middle of this chaos, I could become a new man cleansed of all my sins.
I threw the bags into the air. They flew, their white wings gliding through the maelstrom, carrying salvation to the retching masses.
I could hear the flight attendant screaming, “Those are for Gold Member Elites!” as I pulled myself forward through a tunnel of gagging and noxious fumes.

I say pulled because we were nosediving the wrong way. That metal ass should’ve been down, not up, and I was practically doing chin-ups, one hand crushing the seat in front of me as my legs kicked out into nothingness.
Part of me thought about just letting go and going with God, but then the plane straightened out, and suddenly I had just enough of a chance to get back to my seat.
I ran toward her, wiping streaks of puke from my eyes and smearing it across my forehead like war paint, ignoring the stench and the burn.
There she was. My nun dressed in white. A divine vision.
I held the last bag out for her. An offering. I’d saved it, guarded it, using my body as a human shield against the chaos. And now, with trembling hands, I handed it to her, from sinner to saint.

Our eyes met, and I knew at that moment—this was it. If we made it through this, I’d join the church. I’d convince Carol to give me a second chance. Hell, I’d even cut down on calling her mom a bitch.
I opened my mouth to testify—to tell her about my conversion, my redemption, my shiny new future.
The plane jolted violently, and before she could take the bag, she puked.
I smelled it before I saw it. The unmistakable scent of unfertilized, undigested sulfur. Orange, sack-like over-easy yolks regurgitated from her gullet directly into my face.
I gagged at the taste, the worst thing I’d had in my mouth since Carol’s yeast infection four Christmases ago.

She looked at me. At the bag. At the mess, the filth, the soap, and the puke. Her eyes lingered, taking it all in, and I just knew she saw past it. Past the filth, the stench, whatever was dripping down my leg. She could see what I had done. Who I truly was. Who I could be.
“Your fly is down.”
“For the love of God.”

title: We Won’t Fight
logline: A woman attempts to orchestrate a peaceful family gathering, only to expose the conflicts she hopes to avoid.
subtitle: A full-length stage play by Lindsay Morris

blocks.text: Scene 1
Thursday night. Closing time at a local Jewel. Lindsay browses the wine selection. Greg an employee approaches.
Can I help you find anything?
(Checks name badge)
Hi Greg.
(Shakes hand)
Could you help me find a champagne that would I don't know make my parents like each other again? What pairs well with Xanax?
Uh…
(Laughs nervously)
I don't know about that but I find tequila sometimes does the trick?
It has to be champagne. We’re celebrating.
(picks out a bottle)
What about this one? They look happy.
Actually, it’s a rose. It says it’s on super sale though. 4.99?
Well is it a Chicago wine? My dad wants a Chicago wine. Are there vineyards in Chicago? Maybe on the south side?
I can’t think of any but there’s a lot of Chicago beer.
My dad’s prostate flares up when he drinks beer.
Definitely not beer then.
What’s your favorite champagne, Greg?
Mine?
Yeah. What do you like?
To be honest I don't really drink.
That's perfect. Neither does my family. But when we do we all seem to get along a lot better.
Well.. What’s the occasion?
I’m engineering a positive family experience.
Okay….Is there gonna be food? I hear red wine goes well with/
I mean if my mom cooks I imagine our food will taste like guilt so maybe pizza? (Long pause)I really need this dinner to go well, Greg. What about this one?
The Apothecary Dark? I know it’s wine, and it seems really popular.

When you enter the world of Apothic, you enter the world of intrigue and mystery. Lean into the fantasy. Let us beckon you forward. Apothecary Dark, so full-bodied it can’t be ignored. Does that sound good to you?
Uh…it sounds different ??

My parents are meeting my fiance for the first time. I just want us to get through one dinner where we don't spend the whole time-fighting. That’s not too much to ask? There divorced. I feel like they’ve always been divorced. Are your parents divorced Greg?
My mom’s dead.
Oh. God. How did it happen? I mean. Obviously, you don't have to tell me.
Um.. You know.
But if you want to talk about I’m here for you.
That’s okay.
Anyway, I’m sorry for your loss. Are you married?
Um. Yes. 3 years in March.
Did you get a ring? My boyfriend hasn't bought me a ring yet. He’s going to though. It’s not like he forgot or anything. I mean it doesn't mean anything. Lots of people don't have rings. Right, Greg?
Um. Yes.
I mean you don’t need a ring to buy a dress. Do you? It’s not, as the saleswoman at David Bridals said “jumping the gun”?
And it's not like my family could actually scare him away. Right?
Sure.
But you think it’s a good idea?
People have Family dinners all the time. Cliff. My fiance. He’s normal. He’s from the midwest. Cleveland.
He calls his mom every Thursday. They chat about the weather. The weather Greg. My mom only ever screams about the weather.
We’re closing in a few minutes.
Okay, okay. I’ll take two of these.
And we still need to find that bottle of champagne.
What are you doing around dinner time tomorrow, Greg?
Oh. Um. I’m working.
We should keep in touch. My name’s Lindsay. It’s rare to connect with someone right away. Are you on facebook? Or you an Instagram kind of person?
I think that’s against store policy.
Don’t worry. We’ll keep it on the DL. It’s just been so nice to talk to someone who really understands.
…Yeesh.
Scene 2
Friday morning at Cliff and Lindsay’s apartment. Cliff is packing the wine carefully. Lindsay is moving through piles in search of something.
Have you seen my I.D? I can't find my I.D. anywhere.
Where did you have it last.
It was right. There. I put it on the floor right there.
Why do you keep things on the floor.
That’s where I like them.
Why won't you let me buy you a home organizer?
Because we don't need a home organizer. That's a complete waste of money.
Not if you are keeping things on the floor.
The floor is a perfectly reasonable place to put things.
Says the girl who lost her I.D.
I didn't lose it. You moved it. Where did you put it?
I don't know. I probably put it in a drawer somewhere.
What drawer?
Do you mean the closet?
(LINDSAY begins grabbing items from the closet. She finds her costco ID)
Do you think the airport would accept a Costco ID?
I thought your membership expired.
They don't know that.
What about your passport? Where’s that?
Maybe a library card.
Library cards don't have pictures on them
Can you call American Airlines?
You want me to call them?
Yes. Maybe they can do a one-time exception.
For a library card?
What about a yearbook? I think I still have the one from 8th grade? Have you seen it?
I thought you said you threw that out because your mom said you looked fat in your photo?
She didn't say I was fat she said I could lose a few.
I’ve got a minimum 40 minute hold time. I can see what their website says.
I know what their website says.
Ok. Relax.
I’m super relaxed.
If we miss this flight.
We aren't missing this flight.
I’m just saying that we can always reschedule.
We can’t reschedule.
Why not? I’m sure your Mom would understand.
You mean “your” mom would understand. Do you know what happened when I rescheduled dinner with boyfriend number... Steve?
Yes. You told me.
She wouldn't even let me say his name after that. He was just number 4 like he was one of those kids that the government experimented on in Stranger Things.
I don't think this is a Steve situation
I’m still not allowed to drink Snapple Iced tea. 20 years later and my mom still hasn’t forgiven the lady for rescheduling.
The woman from the commercials? “Made from the best stuff on Earth”
What no? Why would she have a grudge against the actor? I’m talking about the owner.
How does your mom know the owner?
Who knows? But the lady rescheduled and bam. NO more Snapple. Do you know what it was like growing up as a kid in the ’90s and not getting to drink Snapple?
It sounds like your mom isn't the only one who can hold a grudge.
Did the airline pick up yet?
I’m still on hold.
Jesus Cliff. Can’t you remember where you put it?
Did you check your purse?
Of course, I checked my purse.
What about your wallet?
I don’t have a wallet.
We’ll maybe if you had a wallet you wouldn’t always be losing things.
Thank you. What sage words from the guy that can't remember to pick out an engagement ring.
That’s a low blow. I told you it takes time. I don’t want to get you something you’ll hate.
I would never hate anything you picked out.
Are you kidding? I brought home the wrong face wash the other day and you had a meltdown.
Who thinks a charcoal cleansing mask is a face wash?
It’s like this every time you go see your family.
Do you know what my family is gonna say if I don't have a ring?
What will they say?
That you don't love me
(A phone rings. LINDSAY sighs and ignores the call)
Again?
Who was that?...
Who else.
That's the third call this morning.
He keeps forgetting to tell me things.
Anything of importance.
Other than to drink lots of fluids and to avoid airport bathrooms due to the measles outbreak.
That seems like conflicting advice.
Are you caught up on your shots? He’s gonna ask. Make sure you tell him you’ve already had chickenpox. You have had chickenpox, haven't you?
I don’t know.
What do you mean you don't know?
I don't know.
Call your mother. He’ll want proof.
Proof that I’ve had the chickenpox.
Could it have fallen inside a shoe? Have you checked your shoes. Take off your shoes.
(LINDSAY starts taking off Cliff’s shoes)
Are you calling her?
I’m gonna hang up. This is too much.

You think this is too much. I’ve been fielding calls from my father all day. I’ve lost my ID. I terrified a Jewel Osco employee last night and you’re not Jewish. Where in the fuck mother fucking fuck is my ID.
Why does he care if I had chicken pox?
Because of his Shingles. He doesn't want you to make it worse.
That sounds wrong.
CLIFF. Please stop trying to figure out the inner workings of my hypochondriac father and call your mother.
Hey. No matter what happens with your family it isn’t going to change how I feel about you
You haven't met them.
I’ve met you/
/Oh. Oh. What if you put it in your wallet? Where’s your wallet?
Where’s your wallet???
(Cliff points to his jacket)
No. No No…. Omg. Omg. I’m a genius. I knew you touched it.
“Hi Mom. Did I have the Chicken Pox?
Cliff. I found it. I got it. We have to go. We’re gonna miss our flight.
Im asking my mom about the chicken pox. She doesn't know. She’s gone to ask my dad.
Forget the chicken pox. I found my I.D.
But what about the shingles.
Just don't go to the bathroom and you’ll be fine.
Scene 3
A kitchen table is crowded with papers and pills in the absence of family dinners.
A doorbell rings. A dog barks. Sherri screams down from the stairs.
NOAH’S locked out. Answer it or Nora’s gonna keep barking.
Doesn't he live here? Why doesn't he have his own keys?
(The Doorbell rings again and Nora begins barking again)
I don’t want him touching my things when I’m not here. I don’t trust him. Damit the Dog’s barking answer the door.
(NOAH enters)
Do you really think this dinner is a good idea?
Hello to you too.
Fine. Hello.
Where is he?
Who?
Boyfriend number, what are we on 5?
This one isn't getting a number
Is he Jewish?
No.
Then you know he’s getting a number.
Since when did mom start locking you out of the house?
She’s still pissed about the condom. How was I supposed to know Nora was gonna stick her face in the trash and pull out my used jizz bag and bring it to mom. Thank god I tied it off.
UGH (gurgle noises) Dude. Why... I thought she just found the wrapper. Your 27 years old and she’s punishing you for having sex.
Well. At least I was careful. You should be proud of me that I’m not using the pull out method anymore.
That’s not the point. You need to move out.
You don't know what it’s like when you're not here.
Dad calls me 6 times a day too.
It’s not the same. You can ignore his calls. Try ignoring him when he shows up at 3 am, mom won't let him inside and he’s begging you to come out to the car and help him pop his hernia blister.
So again, do you think this dinner’s a good idea?
I don't have a choice.
Are you pregnant?
No, I’m not pregnant. Does it have to be a crisis for us to get together? Can’t it be a good thing?
Do you know if Dad is coming to dinner? He keeps saying he needs to think about it. What is he thinking about?
How should I know? I tried talking to him but he keeps switching the conversation back to his prostate. I can't hear about it anymore.
We need to come up with a game plan.
For what?
To have a normal dinner.
Then why did you invite our family
If we could just team up maybe keep them distracted.
You mean get them drunk enough
It could work... I’m desperate. I’m losing it. Literally. My hair is shedding. Cliff is starting to notice
That your going bald?
No. That I’m freaking out about tomorrow.
You should try these fish oil pills Dad has me on.
Dad already sent me a case last week. Plus you owe me.
I don’t owe you.
Oh yes, you do.
For what?
The thousand dollars I lent you last year when you swore the Giants were gonna win.
You said that was a gift.
A gift you can now repay me for.
I’ll try but you know it's not gonna happen the way you want it to.
Dad listens to you. Just don't start anything with him. Ok. Don't tease him. He hates when you do that. It’s us against them remember.
I can't handle your stress and mine. My app is coming out soon and I need to focus.
(SHERRI comes down the stairs)
Oh please. That app has been (hand air quotations) coming out for the last 2 years.
You don't know what you’re talking about. If you’d just invest a little more money I wouldn't have to keep postponing.
You won’t even tell me what the app does.
I don’t want anyone to steal my idea. It’s on lockdown until I can get a patent lawyer.
And who’s paying for that?
Dad said he might
So he’s your partner now. Does he know what the app is? Because I was the one who convinced him to invest in a fax machine. If you think he’s gonna be better than me go for it.
Dad didn't want to buy a fax machine?
He wouldn't let me use it for the first month. He was worried it might give us cancer. You know he has cancer on his side of the family.
Yeah, Mom, we know.
And depression. That’s where you and NOAH get it from.
I’m not depressed.
You always put on a little weight when you’re stressed.
I thought she was pregnant?
Anything else?
Where’s Clive?
It’s Cliff and he’s at the hotel.
You left him at the hotel!
The plan is that he’s gonna meet the 4 of us at dinner tomorrow.
The four of us?
Yes. The four of us. I invited dad over here.
You invited your father here?? To my house? It’s not Yom Kippur.
Do we need a High Holy Day to sit down and eat dinner as a family?
Yes.
If your father wants to meet Cliff so badly he can take us all out to dinner.
I thought we’d do better in a private setting. Don't you? You do remember my Graduation dinner right?
But we got free cheesecake.
That cause the Cheesecake Factory comped our bill if we would just leave.
We wouldn't have had such a problem if the manager hadn't been such an idiot.
Regardless. I think it would be better if we had it here.
Oh Great. Having your father here…
Don't look at me.
Just promise you guys won't fight.
Why would I fight? What do we have to fight about any more?
That's never seemed to stop you before.
(LINDSAY’s cell phone rings.)
It’s Dad… Again. He keeps calling me.
(she ends the call)
Don't answer it. He always calls when there’s a problem.
Cliff has had all his shots if anyone asks.
Is he a dog?
Just in case Dad asks.
(The house phone rings now)
Now he’s calling the house phone. Tell him if wants to come over here he better bring something decent.I’m not cooking for him.
Mom. Where’s the phone? He’s just gonna keep on calling. Ma!
(SHERRI hands the phone to LINDSAY)
HI, LINDSAY. Can you hear me?
Yes. I can hear you.
Is NOAH with you?
Yeah
Do you know if NOAH did something with my car keys?
How would I know that?
Alright. Shit. I can’t find them. Did you get in alright?
Yes. The flight was fine.
Where’s Cliff. Is he there at the house?
He’s at the hotel.
Did your mother meet him yet?
No mom hasn't met him yet either.
Is she on the phone. Can she hear me?
No she can’t hear you.
You didn't use the bathroom, did you? I just read an article about Laguardia urinals.
No. I didn't use the bathroom at the airport. Besides, I don’t use Urinals.
Swear to God. You’re not lying.
No. I’m not. Why would I lie? Look, Are you coming over for dinner tomorrow or not?
What time is it? Will your mother be there. You know I’m not feeling so great. Is Vicki coming?
I’m only in town for a few days. It’s a family dinner.
Why don't you come over and we can discuss it?
I can't come over now. I have to get back to Cliff.
Please. Come over. I have a bagel I could give you. I need help with my computer.
I really don't have time to help you with your computer today.
But you're smart. You worked for Apple.
I worked at the Apple Store like 10 years ago, and you have a PC. Can you make dinner or not?
You sound congested. Are you sick?
No, I already told you I’m not sick.
Look. Come over. I’ll give you some new supplements. I got. Just come over for an hour. Help me out. Come on.
Okay. Okay. But just for an hour. Because I can't spend all day.
Alright. Well if it’s more than an hour are you going to time me?
No I’m not going to time you.
Tell him to bring a pizza
She wants you to bring a pizza.
What! Can’t she make something?
He wants you to make something.
Why should I make him something? Tell him to pick up a pizza from DiNardos.
SHe wants you to pick one up from DiNardos.
Why can't she make one?
Cause she doesn't want to make one?
Why not. What is she doing?
I don't know why?
Listen. I’m not getting along with the owner of DiNardos at the moment. He’s not gonna want me in there.
You got banned from DiNardos?
He got banned from DiNardos! How did he-
You know what. Forget it. No, we’ll figure something out.
But you're still coming over?
I’m leaving now.
Alright. Cause if your gonna be a few minutes. I’m gonna take a shower.
I’m leaving now
ALright, but if I’m in the shower I’ll leave the door open.
You can’t wait to take a shower?
What. Do you. What are you the shower police? Just come over.
I’m going over to Dad’s.
Good Luck.
Scene 4
Friday evening. Lindsay enters HAMMOND’s apartment. It’s crowded with empty bottles and stacks of newspapers.
Ok. Show me the problem. Ugh. What is, ugh that smell…. It smells like…. Is that? Is that rotting fish.
(LINDSAY walks over to the counter and picks up a bottle of fish oil)
WHAT. NO...I don’t smell anything. Maybe it’s you. Check your shoes? Maybe you stepped in dog garbage?
It’s these. Ugh. You have to refrigerate them.
WHAT. Are you kidding me? I just bought those.
You still need to refrigerate them.

They aren’t rotting. That's what they're supposed to smell like. Why? Do you think there’s something wrong with them? You know I wasn't feeling good this morning. Do you think I should call doctor Finkus? She might be able to fit me in....
Why are you still seeing my old pediatrician?
Why? It doesn't matter.
(HAMMOND smells the container)
There's nothing wrong with it. I trust her. She did a good job with you.
You're fine Dad.
Why are you so annoyed. Did you eat enough? I just pulled out half a power bar from the freezer.
(LINDSAY slips the power bar in her pocket)
Here take this.
(HAMMOND pulls out a bottle of vitamins).
It’s got the blueberry extract. Take it with some warm water….
(He scrambles around his apartment and finds an old crushed up water bottle, half empty)
I’ve got a guy at Vitaworld, he’s very very smart.
Why should I trust him?
Because he’s always there. I can get him on the phone if you want to talk to him.
I don’t want to talk to this guy. Besides. I don't need it. What does Blueberry extract even do?
Sherri, you should take -- -I mean Lindsay. I just called you by your mother's name. I’m all over --. Just take it! You’ll be glad, my guy is smart. He knows his stuff.
Look I need to get this done! I got so much going on at the moment. My throat hurts, I’ve been on the phone all morning with Grandma’s doctor. He didn't even want to talk about my blister/
/Okay.God. I hear you. I’ll take the vitamin and then you can show me what’s wrong with your computer.
You're coming over for dinner tomorrow. Right?
Right. Whatever you want. We can talk about it when you fix the computer.
(LINDSAY and HAMMOND sit down in front of the computer)
(A projected computer screen shows a mess of Icons, obscurely labeled and outdated)
I don't see the problem. What are you trying to do?

Listen. Something happened with my icons. Somebody moved my ICONS, either AOL or the other one. It worked before, I just clicked on it and it appeared. I had a very smart guy set it up. He’s from Apple.
Dad, this is a Gateway PC.

I asked him if he knew you but I don’t have any recent photos. You never give me any photos of you. I forget what you look like. We don’t even have any together. You know I might know where my camera is.
Let's just take care of one thing at a time. What did this guy do?
He set it up just how I like it.
All you are doing is clicking a blank folder. This computer is so slow you really need to get a new one.

No. It's a Supercomputer. He’s a very smart guy, my guy. The brains are very good, inside it's a supercomputer. It’s got “Anti Virus” and “Autocorrect”. I need you to. This guy set it up perfectly … I need to get photos. I don’t want to lose them. But don't look at them. Just open them.
Why don't you ask this guy then? I really don’t know how to help you.

No. Come on. You’re smart. You’re a smart girl. You can figure it out… He isn't answering my calls. He’s got another job. Just get my pictures out. But don't look at them. Sherri-Lindsay. Oh, Jesus. Please come on.
Can't this wait? It really doesn't seem urgent. I have to get back to Cliff, he’s been at the hotel all day.
Sherri. Come On…..

Look. What do you want from me. I’ve had a ROTTEN... A ROTTEN time. You’ve screwed up my whole day. I haven't even taken a shower yet. I gotta go see Dr. Finkus, you insulted my fish oil pills. Will you just. Will you just do it.
Dad! Come over here and pay attention! That way you’ll know how to do it yourself.
Just don't change anything.
First, why are all these files clustered in the corner?
(LINDSAY opens an audio file and Sympathy For The Devil by The Rolling Stones starts playing)

Who gave you that? Did AOL give you that? You know I saw them in concert. Third Row Center at Madison Square Garden. It was my first big show. I bought up a bunch of tickets. Sold them all on the street. NO one had better tickets than me.
I know dad.
I took you to see them. What other 6 years old gets to see The Rolling Stones. Do you remember that?
No…Dad. Is this the file?
(Suddenly all his photos appear, images of a woman dancing topless in the chair Lindsay’s sitting in)
Awwww. Geez. I told you not to look.
Is that Dee Dee? I thought you guys broke up. Why is she naked in this chair? Why would you need these photos? You made me come over to find these Photos! OH God. What is wrong with you?
Just relax. Relax. It’s not a big deal. You’re the one that opened them. Here take a Xanax. Calm Down.
I don’t need a Xanax Dad. I can't do this anymore. I have to go back to the hotel
Wait. Wait. Wait. What did you click. How do I. What button is this?
Dad. I’m leaving I can’t keep doing this with you. Every time it’s the same thing. I just get sucked into your crazy. Can’t you just be a dad for 5 freaking minutes?!
Wait! How do I find the rest of them? Did you move something?
This is my weekend and I can’t spend anymore time helping you find your porn collection.
You shouldn't drive like this. Take a Xanax, you’ll calm down and I’ll see you tomorrow at dinner. And don’t tell your mother.
(Lindsay takes the Xanax)
Fine! Then don't forget the pizza.
Scene 5
Friday night. Back at the hotel, Lindsay walks into the hotel room and collapses on to the bed.
Cliff. Cliff. Are you still here?
Hang on. I’m just washing my hands…
Are you Okay? You look tired. How did things go?
Things went really really well.
Did your family give you a hard time?
Noo. Nooo. I mean it's a little stressful.
It’s always stressful.
It wasn't so bad when I first got here. How long has it been?
Less than day
Oh. That's terrifying.
What have you told them so far?
Nothing. I want to wait until dinner. That way we only have to do it onced.
Are you okay? You seem weirdly calm.
My dad gave me some pills to help.
What pills?
It’s fine.
What did you take?
Blueberry extract, Fish oil, Xanax.
Xanax?
Just so I could drive.
You drove on Xanax.
